title: Different answers
hookLine: a cure, a redemption, a patience, a judgment and an open question, set side by side and not blended
carry: men are disturbed not by the things which happen

cards: Five people sit at one kitchen table. Each has buried someone, or lost a job, or sat up with a fever that wouldn't break. Ask them all the same question: what do you do with suffering?
One talks about a fire that can go out. One talks about a cross. One says a word that means patience.
One says it depends on what you tell yourself. And the last says, honestly, I don't know, and I keep asking. It would be easy to blend those five into one soft sentence.

teach.b: First, the Buddha. In the four noble truths, suffering has a cause, craving, and so it can cease. Buddhists call that ceasing nibbana, and some teachers picture it as a flame that goes out when the fuel is gone.
The answer is a cure: see the cause, walk the path, and the burning cools.

teach.h: THE CROSS: IT CAN BE REDEEMED.
teach.b: Second, the cross. Christians don't explain suffering away. They say that in Jesus, God entered it, and that it can be redeemed, taken up into something that heals.
Revelation looks ahead to a day when "God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes."
Third, the Quran. Hardship is met with sabr, patient endurance, and with prayer: "Seek help in steadfastness and prayer. Lo! Allah is with the steadfast."
And in a short surah, a line said twice in a row: "with hardship goeth ease." Fourth, the Stoics.
Epictetus taught that much of the hurt lives in our judgment. In George Long's translation: "Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things."
Change the judgment, he says, and you change much of the disturbance. Fifth, Job. The book gives no reason at all.
God speaks out of a whirlwind and asks, "Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?"
A cure, a redemption, a patience, a judgment, an open question. Nobody here is asked to make them fit. Each belongs to people who have lived by it on their worst nights.

how: Some people on a spiritual path read several traditions side by side, keeping each answer in its own words, and notice which ones they return to on hard days.

o: one answer to suffering that every religion shares underneath
a debate in which one tradition's answer finally wins out
traditions meeting suffering each in its own voice, unblended

games.q: who answers how — tap the pairs.

s: the book of Job ends by giving Job the reason he suffered
God answers from the whirlwind with questions, not a reason.
the Quran's line about hardship and ease is said twice in a row
the short surah repeats it: with hardship goeth ease.
Epictetus placed much of the disturbance in our opinions about events
in Long's translation: not by the things, but by the opinions about the things.

games.q: a friend in a hard season asks which of the five answers is the right one. how does this year handle it?
o: rank them and pick a winner.
let each speak in its own words, and let her lean.
games.why: this year keeps the answers apart. each tradition speaks for itself, and nobody is told which to choose.

practice: Let the five answers come back one at a time: it can cease; it can be redeemed; patience, and ease with hardship; the judgment is what hurts; the question stays open.
Notice which you lean toward and which you lean away from, and whether one fits a small trouble and another a large one. You don't have to choose; just notice the lean.
